label: GPT-6.1 Terra
output:
Dear Kelechi,

Look at me, buying a stamp because one man decided a voice note was not good enough for him. I hope the people on your train appreciate that you are reading an actual letter, like a Victorian gentleman with a mortgage.

But you said if I was serious about you teaching maths, I should put it in writing. So here we are.

First, I know I brought it up at my birthday, while you were telling us for the hundredth time about another exciting day checking somebody else’s costings. I was teasing you, obviously. But I was also serious.

You’ve been at that firm for nine years now. Nine years of spreadsheets, and from the way you describe them, not even adventurous spreadsheets. I’m not saying being a quantity surveyor doesn’t matter, or that you should walk into the office tomorrow and announce your retirement. You’ve built a career, and that counts for something. But you keep saying you’re bored, and on your last birthday you said, “I just want to do something that matters before 40.” I remember because you weren’t joking when you said it.

I’ve been thinking about that. And I honestly think you should look at teaching.

Before you fold this letter and use it to block the sun through the train window, hear me out.

You’re good at maths, yes. You got an A in further maths, which you have mentioned once or twice since Unilag, in case anyone forgot. But that isn’t the main reason I’m writing. Being good at a subject and being able to help someone else understand it are not the same thing.

I still remember you tutoring half the hostel in Moremi before exams. People would turn up convinced they were finished, and you’d sit there explaining the same thing in three different ways until it made sense. You never made anyone feel stupid for asking again. You’d laugh *with* them, not at them, and somehow they’d leave your room understanding something they had spent a week avoiding.

And then there was my nephew at Christmas. The boy was ready to declare war on fractions until you brought out plates and started dividing imaginary portions of jollof rice. Suddenly he was interested. In fact, he still talks about it, although I suspect the rice helped. You weren’t giving a formal lesson; you just saw that he was stuck and found a way in. That’s a big part of teaching.

You have patience, you’re funny, and you know how to explain things without making people feel small. I can’t promise every teenager will immediately adore you—some of them will test you just because it’s Tuesday—but I think you’d have a good chance of reaching them.

At my school in Peckham, we’ve had a supply teacher covering two Year 9 maths groups since September. We have about 1,100 kids, and there’s always a lot going on, but it’s hard for pupils when they don’t have the same person with them consistently. I’m not telling you this to make you feel guilty or suggest you must come and rescue us. I’m saying there are young people who need good maths teachers, and you have qualities that could make you one.

Last month, one of my Year 11s, Damola, finally got simultaneous equations after three weeks of wrestling with them. He looked at his page, looked at me and shouted, “Is that all??” The whole class clapped. I laughed because, after three weeks, the answer was very much *not* “that’s all.” But seeing his face when it clicked was brilliant. He sat up differently for the rest of the lesson. Those moments don’t happen every day, and they don’t make the paperwork disappear, but they stay with you.

Now, because I know you: no, I have not forgotten to mention the hard parts.

Teaching is hard. The marking can feel endless. Behaviour is wahala on some days, and there are afternoons when you’ve explained the same thing repeatedly, dealt with three different problems and still have a pile of work waiting for you. You can plan what you think is a beautiful lesson and watch it fall flat by 9:15. Holidays are a benefit, yes, but they don’t mean the weeks in between are easy.

When I started in 2019, I cried in the car park twice in my first term. Twice, Kelechi. Once I even checked whether anyone had seen me before driving off. I don’t tell you that to put you off; I’m telling you because I don’t want to sell you a version of the job that doesn’t exist. It got better as I learned, asked for help and found my feet. I still have difficult days, but I also have days when I come home knowing exactly why I do it.

There would be practical things to think about too. The salaried training route I mentioned means you’d be paid while you train over one year, starting in September 2027. There would still be a pay drop in that first year, and you’d need to look properly at what that means for you. I’m not going to wave away your bills with a speech about following your passion. There are the holidays and pension to consider, and the pay goes up, but you should get the actual details and decide whether the numbers work. I know better than to bring vague numbers to a quantity surveyor.

And please don’t start with “I’m too old.” You’re 34, not 94. A woman in my department started teaching at 41 and is doing brilliantly. You’ve spent nine years working, dealing with people and solving problems; you wouldn’t be turning up with nothing just because the classroom is new to you.

Here is what I’m asking, and it is not for you to hand in your notice or sign anything. Come to the open evening at the training partnership in Lewisham on **Thursday 19 November 2026 at 6pm**. Applications for next September open soon, so it’s a good chance to ask about the salaried route, the pay, the workload and anything else you want to know. Ask the awkward questions too. Especially the awkward questions.

I’ll come with you. Afterwards, if you decide it’s not for you, I’ll accept it. I may still make occasional comments about your spreadsheets, but that is my right as your friend.

I just don’t want you to dismiss the idea with a laugh before you’ve looked at it. You were there for so many of us at Unilag when we thought we couldn’t understand something. I’ve seen you do the same with my nephew. I think you might find something in teaching that you’ve been missing, and I’d love for you to give yourself the chance to find out.

Let me know about the 19th. You can reply by text; I won’t insist on a handwritten letter. I’m not wicked.

Your friend,  
The one who actually bought a stamp
